scenario: Drafting a comparison post: the writer verifies every statistic against its primary source and links to that source inline before publishing.
The post's byline names the author and a two-sentence bio establishing their hands-on experience with the topic.
Before publishing a near-duplicate of an older post on the same domain, the writer sets a canonical tag pointing to the older, canonical URL.
Every image in the draft has meaningful alt text, and purely decorative images are marked with empty alt attributes.
The draft leads with the answer the reader needs, uses short sentences, and defines an acronym the audience wouldn't already know.
Article structured data (author, datePublished, dateModified, publisher) is added and matches exactly what's visible on the rendered page.
The post claims a product is '#1 fastest on the market' with no benchmark, source, or internal data to back the claim.
The byline reads only 'Team' with no named author, on a topic where the reader needs to know who's speaking and why they're credible.
The same article is published at two URLs on the same site with no canonical tag on either, letting them compete for the same query.
The document skips from an <h2> straight to an <h4> to make a subheading look smaller, with no <h3> in between.
Article schema on the page declares an author name that does not match the byline actually shown to readers.
The post is pushed live without checking that its internal links resolve or that its statistics still link to a live source.
A large batch of near-identical posts is auto-generated by lightly rewording existing top-ranking articles on the same queries, with no original data, example, or firsthand angle added.
